Gateshead Productivity, 2024

Labour productivity is the value of what the borough produces for each hour worked or each job filled. This dashboard covers Gateshead's output per hour and per job from 2002 to 2024 against the seven NEMSA authorities, the wider North East, Gateshead's ONS economic statistical neighbours and the UK. It is built on the ONS subregional productivity release of , which adds 2024 and revises every earlier year.

GVA per hour worked, current price, smoothed, index UK = 100. Gateshead and the NEMSA area are local authority and combined authority tables. The North East region is the published ITL1 figure (unsmoothed).

About This Dashboard

Measures

  • GVA per hour worked is balanced gross value added at current basic prices divided by total hours worked in the area. It is the ONS headline measure of labour productivity. Hours are workplace based, so they count people working in Gateshead wherever they live
  • GVA per filled job is the same GVA divided by productivity jobs (employees, the self-employed, HM Armed Forces and government-supported trainees), workplace based. It does not allow for differences in hours, so areas with more part-time work look less productive on it
  • Index (UK = 100) compares an area with the UK less Extra-Regio in the same year. A fall in the index means the area grew more slowly than the UK, not necessarily that its productivity fell
  • Smoothed figures are a weighted five-year moving average calculated by ONS. Local authority figures are published smoothed only, because single years are too volatile. ONS says revisions are typically largest for the previous year, because of new input data
  • Current price figures include inflation, so they are for comparing areas in the same year. Growth in current price figures is cash growth, not real growth
  • Indicative real output per hour is our calculation. It divides chained volume GVA ( money value) from the complete September 2026 regional accounts by the published productivity hours. ONS does not publish real terms productivity for local authorities, because it judges the single-year data too volatile, and our series is unsmoothed. Treat it as an indication of direction, not a measured rate. For NEMSA, the North East region and the UK the real terms figures shown are the published ONS series
  • Productivity hours are average weekly hours worked in the area, and productivity jobs are filled jobs, both constrained by ONS to its regional and UK totals

    Notes and Caveats

    • These are official statistics in development. The ONS release badges the regional and subregional productivity series this way, and the methods are still changing
    • This edition constrains regional and local hours and jobs to the new UK totals from the ONS component approach to measuring labour input, published on 17 November 2026. The UK hours and jobs were revised down, which raises productivity levels in pounds in almost every year. ONS will review how it apportions hours to regions and local areas before next year's release, which may bring further revisions
    • Every year is revised in this edition, so pound figures here should not be set beside figures from the previous edition. Products that quote Gateshead's 2023 output per hour as £ are on the previous edition
    • The Labour Force Survey and Annual Population Survey feed the hours estimates. ONS notes their quality was reduced from mid-2023 and through 2024 because of falling sample sizes
    • Local productivity figures are affected by unmeasured differences in prices between areas, and by how ONS allocates the output of firms with many sites. The second matters more for small areas
    • GVA is allocated by economic ownership, so output UK companies produce abroad can be counted in UK GVA. ONS notes that recent upward revisions in pharmaceuticals show up as higher labour productivity, allocated across UK branch locations
    • ONS says its hours measure is in a transitional state while the component approach is brought in, and used output per job rather than per hour for its own growth analysis this year
    • ONS publishes no confidence intervals for these figures, so no error bars are drawn. They are modelled estimates built partly on surveys, so they carry real uncertainty that the charts cannot show, and small differences between areas should not be read as meaningful
    • Northern Ireland jobs for 2024 are not published at local authority level, so Northern Ireland authorities have no 2024 output per job
    • The Isles of Scilly are not published. England ranks are out of the English authorities with figures and UK ranks out of the UK authorities with figures
    • Barnsley and Sheffield carry their 2025 codes in the productivity tables and their earlier codes in the GVA tables. The build matches them
